winner_protocol:
Age: 45  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Penetrating stab wound to the left anterior chest with signs of obstructive shock  

Analysis: The panel unanimously identified acute cardiac tamponade due to hemopericardium from a left‑anterior penetrating stab wound. All experts agreed on the classic presentation (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, FAST showing pericardial effusion with right‑ventricular diastolic collapse) and on the physiologic mechanism of obstructive shock that can progress to cardiac arrest within minutes. Consensus was reached that definitive management is an emergency left anterolateral thoracotomy performed in the emergency department; pericardiocentesis is only a temporizing bridge when thoracotomy cannot be obtained within seconds. Divergence occurred regarding adjunctive bedside diagnostics: Experts A and C argued that no further testing should be performed before thoracotomy to avoid any delay, whereas Expert B recommended ultra‑rapid portable chest X‑ray and 12‑lead ECG only if they can be obtained in parallel without postponing the surgical decompression. This difference was noted and incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Portable ultrasound (FAST) already performed; cardiac monitor for arrhythmia detection; rapid‑sequence intubation equipment; massive transfusion protocol supplies; spinal immobilization board; portable chest X‑ray unit (if immediately available without delaying thoracotomy); 12‑lead ECG machine (if immediately available); arterial line kit for invasive blood pressure monitoring; large‑bore IV or central line access; blood gas analyzer (if already in use).  

Conclusion: Acute cardiac tamponade from penetrating left‑anterior chest trauma causing life‑threatening obstructive shock; requires emergent surgical decompression.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  

Recommendations: Activate the emergency‑department trauma team immediately and notify trauma/general surgery and cardiothoracic surgery. Proceed without delay to an emergency left anterolateral thoracotomy in the ED as the definitive initial intervention. Do not perform pericardiocentesis unless thoracotomy cannot be initiated within seconds; if attempted, it is only a brief bridge. Maintain spinal immobilization until cervical spine injury is excluded. Initiate massive transfusion protocol given the high likelihood of significant internal hemorrhage. Prepare for rapid‑sequence intubation if mental status deteriorates further. Begin continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias and obtain a 12‑lead ECG and portable chest X‑ray only if they can be completed concurrently with preparation for thoracotomy and will not postpone the incision. After thoracotomy, assess for concurrent injuries such as left anterior descending coronary artery or internal mammary artery laceration, myocardial or ventricular wall laceration, and valvular damage. Ensure vigilant post‑decompression hemodynamic monitoring for re‑accumulation of pericardial fluid, recurrent bleeding, or ongoing tamponade. Provide postoperative intensive care with ongoing transfusion support, ventilatory management, and cardiac monitoring.  

Notes: The minimal external bleeding does not rule out massive intrapericardial hemorrhage. Clear lung fields on exam do not exclude a small pneumothorax or hemothorax; a chest X‑ray after stabilization is prudent. An ECG may show low voltage or electrical alternans, supporting the diagnosis, but should not delay thoracotomy.

Age: 41  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Unintentional 10‑kg weight loss over 2 months, heat intolerance, palpitations with mild exertion, frequent loose stools, irritability, difficulty concentrating at work, gritty sensation in both eyes, mild proptosis, tremor, diaphoresis, calf cramps and proximal muscle weakness.  

Analysis: The patient’s clinical picture (weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tachycardia, tremor, diaphoresis, diffuse goiter with bruit, mild thyroid eye disease) together with laboratory findings (suppressed TSH <0.01 µU/mL, markedly elevated free T4 and free T3, positive TSH‑receptor antibodies) is diagnostic of primary hyperthyroidism due to Graves disease. The technetium‑99m uptake scan (not shown) is presumed to demonstrate diffusely increased uptake, further confirming Graves disease and excluding thyroiditis or factitious thyrotoxicosis. All three experts agreed on this diagnosis and on the need for non‑emergent, specialty‑driven care. Points of divergence were noted: Experts A and B advocated initiating methimazole after baseline laboratory assessment, whereas Expert C recommended deferring antithyroid medication until an endocrinology consultation. Imaging preferences also differed: Expert A emphasized orbital CT/MRI to gauge ophthalmopathy severity; Expert B suggested an echocardiogram if tachycardia persists and a pituitary MRI only if TSH were inappropriately normal; Expert C mentioned a thyroid ultrasound to document goiter size and exclude nodules. These differences are incorporated into the diagnostic work‑up and management plan.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, liver function tests, fasting glucose and HbA1c, repeat TSH, free T4 and free T3, TSH‑receptor antibody assay (already obtained), 12‑lead ECG (already obtained), transthoracic echocardiogram if tachycardia or cardiac symptoms persist, high‑resolution orbital CT or MRI if eye symptoms worsen, thyroid ultrasound to document gland size and exclude nodules, repeat technetium‑99m uptake scan (already performed), and a formal ophthalmology examination with visual acuity and intra‑ocular pressure measurement.  

Conclusion: Primary hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) with mild thyroid eye disease.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Begin symptomatic control with a non‑selective beta‑blocker (e.g., propranolol 20–40 mg PO q6–8 h) to reduce tachycardia, tremor and anxiety. Obtain baseline CBC, liver enzymes, renal function, fasting glucose/HbA1c, and repeat ECG before any antithyroid drug. Arrange prompt referral to an endocrinologist; after specialist evaluation, initiate methimazole (15–30 mg PO daily) with close monitoring for agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity. Counsel the patient to cease smoking immediately, as tobacco use accelerates Graves ophthalmopathy. Coordinate care with ophthalmology for baseline and follow‑up orbital assessment; obtain orbital imaging if visual changes or optic nerve compression are suspected. Review sertraline for potential interaction with methimazole (generally safe but monitor for serotonergic side effects). Monitor glycemic status given the mild hyperglycemia that may be thyrotoxic‑induced; repeat fasting glucose/HbA1c in 4–6 weeks. Evaluate calf cramps and proximal weakness as thyrotoxic myopathy; these should improve with euthyroidism. Consider a baseline transthoracic echocardiogram to rule out tachycardia‑induced cardiomyopathy, especially if heart rate remains >100 bpm after beta‑blockade. Perform a thyroid ultrasound to document goiter dimensions and exclude occult nodules. Discuss definitive therapy (radioactive iodine ablation or thyroidectomy) after achieving euthyroid status, taking into account the patient’s occupational need for rapid symptom control and his smoking status. Ensure ongoing psychiatric follow‑up for depression, recognizing that mood may improve with treatment of hyperthyroidism but may still require adjustment of sertraline or additional therapy.  

Notes: Family history of autoimmune thyroid disease supports a genetic predisposition; Gilbert syndrome does not alter management. The patient’s occupational impairment underscores the importance of timely initiation of therapy and close follow‑up.

Age: 45  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Acute onset pain, redness, and swelling of the pretibial lower leg with low‑grade fever  

Analysis: The presentation is classic for acute cellulitis of the lower leg, characterized by erythema, edema, tenderness, and a modest fever. All three experts agreed on this primary diagnosis and on the need for prompt outpatient evaluation, while differing on the urgency label: Expert B emphasized that low‑grade fever alone does not constitute an emergency, whereas Expert C warned that fever may herald rapid progression and thus advocated a cautious, urgent approach. The Delphi consensus resolved this by classifying the case as non‑emergent care, with the understanding that emergent criteria apply only if red‑flag features (systemic toxicity, rapidly expanding erythema, severe pain out of proportion, bullae, necrosis, crepitus, hypotension, or signs of necrotizing infection) develop. Consensus also existed on the core differential diagnoses (deep‑vein thrombosis, erysipelas, contact or stasis dermatitis, gout, necrotizing soft‑tissue infection, infected ulcer), the baseline laboratory work‑up (CBC, CRP/ESR, basic metabolic panel, vital signs), and the first‑line oral antibiotic regimen (cephalexin). Divergence remained regarding MRSA risk assessment, alternative empiric coverage, and advanced imaging when necrotizing infection is suspected but bedside ultrasound is inconclusive. These points are incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CBC with differential, C‑reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate, basic metabolic panel, full set of vital signs, bedside high‑frequency ultrasound of the affected area, lower‑extremity duplex ultrasound if deep‑vein thrombosis is suspected, blood cultures only if systemic signs worsen, ankle‑brachial index or pulse examination for peripheral arterial disease, MRI or CT of the leg if necrotizing fasciitis is strongly suspected and ultrasound is nondiagnostic.  

Conclusion: Acute cellulitis of the pretibial lower leg in a 45‑year‑old man; currently classified as non‑emergent care.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  

Recommendations: Initiate oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5–7 days, adjusting dose for renal function if needed. If the patient has a documented β‑lactam allergy, prescribe clindamycin 300 mg every 6 hours or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; consider TMP‑SMX or linezolid if MRSA risk factors (recent hospitalization, prior MRSA infection, close contact with livestock, injection drug use) are present. Obtain a thorough history for recent skin trauma, breaks, ulceration, tinea pedis, chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema, diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, immunosuppression, prior cellulitis episodes, recent antibiotic exposure, and medication use that may affect immunity. Document allergy status, especially β‑lactam hypersensitivity, and verify tetanus immunization; administer tetanus booster if indicated. Perform a complete vital‑sign assessment (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature) to identify early systemic involvement. Evaluate peripheral pulses and, if arterial disease is suspected, measure the ankle‑brachial index. Assess social factors such as occupation, animal exposure, or travel that could suggest atypical pathogens. Arrange follow‑up in 48–72 hours, either in person or via telehealth, with explicit instructions to return sooner for worsening pain, expanding erythema, new fever, bullae, crepitus, or any systemic symptoms. Refer to Infectious Disease, Surgery, or Dermatology if red‑flag signs appear, if there is no clinical improvement after 48–72 hours, or if comorbidities (diabetes, immunosuppression, peripheral vascular disease) increase the risk of complications. Educate the patient on limb elevation, skin hygiene, treatment of any concurrent tinea pedis, completion of the antibiotic course, and wound care if a break is present. Emphasize early recognition of complications and preventive measures such as regular moisturization, avoidance of trauma, and prompt treatment of interdigital fungal infections.  

Notes: Maintain a low threshold for imaging (MRI/CT) if necrotizing infection is suspected despite an inconclusive ultrasound. Document all findings and reassess risk stratification at each follow‑up visit.

Conclusion: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) – self‑limited, no immediate need for antibiotics or further investigations.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations: Provide supportive care—rest, adequate hydration, analgesic/antipyretic (acetaminophen or ibuprofen), saline nasal irrigation, and honey or steam inhalation for cough relief. Educate the patient that antibiotics will not help a viral illness and discuss the importance of antibiotic stewardship, using his prior prescription as a teaching point. Offer smoking‑cessation counseling, emphasizing that tobacco use can prolong symptoms, increase risk of secondary bacterial infection, and worsen future respiratory health. Review and update vaccination status (influenza, COVID‑19, Tdap) and recommend immunization if pending. Advise the patient to seek re‑evaluation if fever >38.5 °C, development of purulent sputum, worsening dyspnea, new chest findings, or any other red‑flag symptoms. If the patient has underlying asthma, COPD, or other chronic lung disease, a brief baseline respiratory assessment (spirometry or peak flow) may be warranted. Mention that immunocompromised states (e.g., HIV, chronic steroid use) would alter urgency and testing needs; obtain relevant history to rule these out.  

Notes: Monitor for early signs of bacterial superinfection (sinusitis, acute bronchitis) and instruct the patient to report new localized pain, nasal discharge changes, or prolonged cough beyond 10 days.

Despite these variations, the core diagnostic consensus remained unchanged.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for the initial assessment; diagnosis is clinical based on history and physical examination.  

Conclusion: Acute irritant contact dermatitis (razor burn) of the neck.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Advise the patient to cease shaving the affected area until the skin has healed. Apply cool compresses to the neck for comfort and reduce inflammation. Use a fragrance‑free, gentle moisturizer or barrier ointment after cleansing, and apply a low‑potency topical corticosteroid such as 1 % hydrocortisone cream twice daily for up to three days if inflammation persists. Emphasize proper shaving technique: use a sharp, clean razor; lubricate the skin with shaving cream or gel; shave in the direction of hair growth; avoid excessive pressure; and moisturize the skin before and after shaving. Inquire about recent use of new soaps, detergents, or other skin products that could act as co‑irritants, and consider a patch test if an allergic component is suspected, especially if symptoms do not improve within five to seven days. Counsel the patient that mild warmth is typical of inflammation and not indicative of infection; however, advise immediate medical review if any of the following develop: pustules, spreading erythema, increasing pain, fever, chills, or regional lymphadenopathy. Should secondary bacterial infection be suspected, obtain a skin culture and initiate appropriate topical or systemic antibiotics. Schedule a follow‑up or advise the patient to return for evaluation if symptoms persist beyond one week or worsen despite self‑care measures.  

Notes: The patient’s young age and lack of prior dermatologic history suggest a low likelihood of chronic skin disease, but underlying atopic or sensitive skin may increase susceptibility to irritant reactions. Education on shaving habits and product selection is essential to prevent recurrence.

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as a first‑degree (superficial) sunburn based on the history of 5 hours of beach exposure without sunscreen reapplication, the well‑demarcated erythema matching swimsuit lines, warmth, tenderness, and the absence of blistering, systemic symptoms, or signs of infection. Minor differences among experts include: Expert A emphasized that dermatology referral is optional for complications, Expert B highlighted specific red‑flag features that would prompt urgent care, and Expert C noted that general medicine can also manage uncomplicated cases. All experts concur on the core management of cool compresses, moisturizers, oral analgesics, hydration, and sun avoidance.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; diagnosis is clinical.  

Conclusion: First‑degree sunburn (superficial erythema) limited to shoulders, upper back, and posterior neck; self‑care appropriate.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Provide cool (not ice‑cold) compresses to the affected areas and apply soothing moisturizers such as aloe vera or fragrance‑free emollients. Offer oral analgesia with ibuprofen or acetaminophen as needed for pain. Encourage liberal oral hydration and advise avoidance of further sun exposure until the erythema resolves. Counsel the patient on proper sunscreen use: apply a broad‑spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher 15‑30 minutes before sun exposure, use a sufficient amount (approximately one ounce for the whole body), and reapply every two hours or after swimming, sweating, or towel drying. Recommend protective clothing, wide‑brim hats, and limiting outdoor activities between 10 am and 4 pm. Inquire about photosensitizing medications (e.g., tetracyclines, retinoids, sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones) and document any recent use. Ask the patient’s Fitzpatrick skin type to assess burn susceptibility and discuss heightened risk for individuals with type I or II. Obtain a brief skin cancer and family history, noting any prior severe or recurrent sunburns, atypical nevi, or personal history of melanoma. Screen for underlying dermatologic conditions (eczema, psoriasis) that may impair barrier function, and assess for immunocompromised states (HIV, transplant, systemic steroids) that could increase infection risk. Query recent exposure to new detergents, fabrics, or topical products that might cause allergic contact dermatitis. Educate on long‑term risks of cumulative UV exposure, including photo‑aging and melanoma, and emphasize the importance of consistent sun protection to prevent future burns. Advise the patient to return for evaluation if any red‑flag signs develop: blistering, fever, chills, increasing pain, spreading erythema, pus, or systemic symptoms such as nausea or dizziness.  

Notes: No follow‑up appointment is required for uncomplicated cases; the patient should be instructed to seek care if symptoms worsen or red‑flags appear.

The panel diverged on the urgency of care: Experts A and C classified the situation as requiring emergent care, emphasizing the time‑sensitive nature of testicular cancer, whereas Expert B considered it non‑emergent but time‑sensitive, suggesting a prompt outpatient referral rather than immediate emergency department evaluation. The consensus label resolves this disagreement in favor of emergent care, reflecting the highest priority assigned by the majority of expert judgments. - Staging imaging after diagnosis: contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, chest X‑ray or CT, and possibly MRI of the pelvis if indicated  
- Fertility assessment (semen analysis) and discussion of sperm banking prior to definitive therapy

Subclinical specialization: Urology

Complaint: Fever, nausea, vomiting, sore throat with exudative pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy; rapid antigen test positive for group A Streptococcus  

Analysis: The clinical picture (abrupt fever, sore throat, exudates, tender cervical nodes) together with a positive rapid antigen test confirms acute streptococcal pharyngitis caused by group A Streptococcus. All experts agreed on this diagnosis and on the classification as non‑emergent, suitable for outpatient pediatric care. Consensus also aligned on the need for a 10‑day course of oral penicillin or amoxicillin, the lack of necessity for further microbiologic testing after a positive rapid test, and the importance of supportive measures (hydration, antipyretics). Minor differences emerged in the framing of differential diagnoses: Expert B focused on the sufficiency of the rapid test, while Expert C listed viral etiologies (adenovirus, EBV) and rare considerations (peritonsillar abscess, HIV) as alternative possibilities if the clinical course deviates. No expert raised emergent red‑flag signs, and all concurred that such signs would mandate urgent evaluation.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Rapid antigen detection test (already performed); throat culture only if rapid test were negative or if there is treatment failure; consider heterophile antibody test for EBV if symptoms persist beyond the expected course or splenomegaly develops.  

Conclusion: Acute group A streptococcal pharyngitis, uncomplicated, in a 7‑year‑old child.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Initiate oral penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days as first‑line therapy. If the child has a documented penicillin allergy, use a first‑generation cephalosporin (if not anaphylactic) or a macrolide such as azithromycin. Provide supportive care with adequate hydration, antipyretics (acetaminophen or ibuprofen), and a soft diet; throat lozenges may be used if age‑appropriate. Counsel the family to complete the full antibiotic course, to keep the child home from school until at least 24 hours after initiation of antibiotics and fever resolution, and to monitor for red‑flag symptoms (stridor, drooling, severe neck swelling, trismus, uvular deviation, toxic appearance, persistent high fever >48‑72 h). Advise immediate medical attention if any of these develop.  

Address additional considerations: Be alert for co‑existing viral infections (influenza, COVID‑19) that may alter the clinical picture; if atypical features such as conjunctival injection, extremity changes, or rash appear, evaluate for Kawasaki disease. A family history of rheumatic fever or post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis warrants reinforced counseling on adherence and follow‑up. In cases of recurrent streptococcal infections, consider referral for tonsillectomy evaluation or immunologic assessment. If symptoms persist beyond the expected course or splenomegaly emerges, obtain heterophile antibody testing for EBV.  

Notes: No immediate ENT referral is required unless complications (peritonsillar abscess, airway obstruction) arise or the infection fails to improve after 48‑72 hours of appropriate therapy.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Establish exact time of symptom onset or last known well to determine eligibility for IV alteplase (≤ 4.5 hours) and thrombectomy (up to 24 hours for selected patients). Evaluate cardiac source with ECG and consider transesophageal echocardiography for left atrial thrombus. Review comorbidities such as diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, and renal function to guide post‑acute anticoagulation decisions (e.g., transition to a direct oral anticoagulant if appropriate). Complaint: Itchy red rash on both wrists for 4 days, localized to the area of a new costume‑jewelry bracelet, without blistering, weeping, or spread.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as allergic contact dermatitis, most likely due to nickel in the costume jewelry. The history of a new metal exposure, well‑demarcated erythematous patches, and the absence of systemic signs support this diagnosis. Consensus was reached on the non‑urgent nature of the condition, the appropriateness of self‑care as the initial management level, and Dermatology as the specialty for further evaluation if needed. The experts also agreed on the key differentials (irritant contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea corporis, early cellulitis) and on red‑flag features that would require escalation. A point of divergence arose from Expert B, who noted that the questionnaire lacked an explicit follow‑up timeline and specific guidance on arranging patch testing; this gap was incorporated into the final recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No immediate tests are required; diagnosis is clinical. Consider patch testing if the rash recurs or the allergen remains uncertain, and a KOH preparation only if a fungal infection is suspected.  

Conclusion: Allergic contact dermatitis secondary to nickel exposure from the bracelet.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  

Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Remove the bracelet immediately and apply a low‑ to medium‑potency topical corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone 1 % or triamcinolone 0.1 % to the affected areas twice daily. Use fragrance‑free moisturizers to restore the skin barrier and take an oral antihistamine if itching interferes with daily activities. Educate the patient to avoid the offending jewelry and all nickel‑containing items; recommend nickel‑free alternatives or barrier methods such as applying clear nail polish to the jewelry surface. Discuss the possibility of cross‑reactivity with cobalt or chromium and advise vigilance with other metal exposures. Inform the patient that the rash should improve within 1–2 weeks after allergen removal; if it does not, or if it worsens, schedule a follow‑up visit in 7–10 days. Advise the patient to return sooner if any red‑flag signs develop, including vesiculation, spreading beyond the wrists, increasing pain, fever, signs of infection (purulence, warmth, swelling, lymphangitic streaking), or systemic allergic symptoms such as angioedema or respiratory distress. If the rash persists beyond the initial treatment period, arrange referral to Dermatology for patch testing, which is the gold‑standard for identifying specific metal allergens; the primary‑care provider can initiate the referral and coordinate testing timing. Counsel the patient that chronic or repeated exposure can lead to lichenification or secondary bacterial infection, and that early treatment of any such complications is essential.  

Notes: Nickel allergy affects up to 20 % of women and is the most common cause of contact dermatitis from costume jewelry. Barrier creams may be useful when avoidance is not feasible.

Analysis: All three experts agreed that the presentation is classic for recurrent herpes simplex labialis (HSV‑1) based on the prodromal tingling, vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border, and the stress‑related recurrence pattern. The condition is non‑urgent and can be managed with self‑care. Consensus was reached on the key differentials (impetigo, contact dermatitis, angular cheilitis, aphthous ulcer, herpes zoster, pemphigus vulgaris, hand‑foot‑mouth disease) and on red‑flag features that would require urgent referral (fever, extensive or necrotic lesions, ocular involvement, facial nerve palsy, immunocompromise). All experts agreed that routine diagnostic testing is unnecessary for a classic case; laboratory confirmation (PCR, viral culture, Tzanck smear) is reserved for atypical presentations or immunocompromised patients.  

A point of divergence was the preferred first‑line antiviral strategy. Expert A and Expert C noted that both oral and topical antivirals are acceptable, with oral agents offering greater efficacy, while Expert B advocated oral antivirals as the primary choice for most patients. The panel leaned toward oral antiviral therapy as the preferred initial treatment, acknowledging that topical therapy remains an option for very mild lesions or patient preference.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for typical recurrent herpes labialis. Reserve PCR, viral culture, or Tzanck smear for atypical lesions, immunocompromised hosts, or diagnostic uncertainty.  

Conclusion: Recurrent herpes simplex labialis (HSV‑1 cold sore).  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate oral antiviral therapy promptly, ideally within 72 hours of symptom onset; valacyclovir 2 g twice daily for one day (or 1 g twice daily for one day) is recommended for most patients. For very mild lesions or if oral therapy is contraindicated, topical acyclovir 5 % applied five times daily may be used as an adjunct or alternative. Provide supportive care with cold compresses, analgesics, and lip moisturizers. Counsel the patient on red‑flag signs (fever, lymphadenopathy, extensive or necrotic lesions, ocular pain, vision changes, facial weakness) and advise immediate medical evaluation if any appear.  

Address additional considerations:  
- Assess immune status (HIV testing, review of steroids, chemotherapy, or other immunosuppressive agents).  
- Inquire about current or planned pregnancy; avoid acyclovir in the first trimester and consider safety profiles of valacyclovir.  
- Screen for ocular symptoms (pain, photophobia, visual changes) to rule out herpetic keratitis; refer to ophthalmology if present.  
- Emphasize hand hygiene and avoidance of touching the eyes or other mucosal surfaces to prevent autoinoculation (e.g., herpetic whitlow, keratitis).  
- Review medication history for allergies or interactions (e.g., probenecid) before prescribing antivirals.  
- Discuss transmission risk: avoid kissing, sharing utensils, or oral contact during active lesions; use barrier protection if contact is unavoidable.  
- Verify varicella vaccination status to exclude VZV as a cause of vesicular lesions.  
- If recurrences become frequent (≥4 per year) or particularly severe, consider suppressive antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 500 mg daily) and arrange follow‑up with dermatology for evaluation.  

Notes: Patient education on stress‑reduction techniques, regular use of lip balm with SPF 30+, and avoidance of known triggers (UV exposure, lip trauma) should be reinforced to reduce future reactivations.

Complaint: Acute worsening lower back pain with bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, and gait instability.  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of cauda equina syndrome secondary to a large central L4‑L5 disc herniation, confirmed by MRI. All experts agreed on the diagnosis and the need for urgent surgical decompression within 24–48 hours. Consensus was reached on the emergency classification (Requires emergent care) and the subclinical specialization (Neurology). Divergence occurred regarding the necessity of additional imaging; while some participants initially considered a contingency CT myelogram, the final consensus, driven by Expert C’s rationale and subsequent outlier review, concluded that MRI alone is sufficient when diagnostic and readily available. Minor differences in urgency wording were harmonized to the agreed 24‑hour target.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the lumbar spine (already obtained), baseline laboratory studies including CBC, BMP, coagulation panel, inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) to screen for infection, medication review for anticoagulant/antiplatelet agents, documentation of baseline bowel and bladder function, and continuous bladder monitoring.  

Conclusion: Cauda equina syndrome due to a central L4‑L5 disc herniation requiring emergent surgical decompression.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  

Recommendations: Admit the patient to a monitored unit. Place a Foley catheter for bladder drainage and begin a bladder monitoring schedule. Initiate analgesia, keep the patient NPO, provide IV fluids, and consider a short course of IV steroids. Start DVT prophylaxis. Obtain a thorough medication history to identify anticoagulant or antiplatelet use and coordinate reversal or holding of these agents per institutional protocol. Document baseline bowel function and start a bowel regimen with stool softeners and scheduled laxatives. Optimize comorbidities such as diabetes, chronic steroid use, obesity, and cardiovascular disease before surgery; provide stress‑dose steroids if indicated. Exclude alternative pathologies (spinal epidural abscess, metastatic disease, transverse myelitis) by reviewing clinical signs (fever, weight loss), inflammatory markers, and, if suspicion arises, ordering contrast‑enhanced MRI or relevant labs. If MRI were unavailable or nondiagnostic, arrange an emergent CT myelogram. Consult neurosurgery or orthopedic spine surgery immediately for operative planning. Perform urgent decompressive laminectomy and discectomy at L4‑L5 within 24 hours, no later than 48 hours from symptom onset. Postoperatively, continue ICU or step‑down monitoring, maintain bladder management with a weaning plan, continue bowel regimen, provide DVT prophylaxis, encourage early mobilization, and initiate physical and occupational therapy. Arrange follow‑up with neurosurgery and rehabilitation medicine, and counsel the patient regarding possible persistent bladder, bowel, or sexual dysfunction.  

Notes: Symptom duration beyond 48 hours is associated with poorer neurological recovery; therefore, any further delay must be avoided. Prior spine surgeries or instrumentation may alter the surgical approach and should be reviewed pre‑operatively.

Conclusion: The presentation is consistent with delayed onset muscle soreness, a self‑limited condition that typically resolves within 5‑7 days with appropriate self‑care.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations: Advise the patient to continue gentle activity such as light walking and low‑impact movements, incorporate gentle stretching, and apply heat after the first 48 hours to relieve discomfort. Ensure adequate hydration and encourage intake of sufficient protein and overall nutrition to support muscle recovery. Educate the patient that DOMS is benign and self‑limited, and outline clear red‑flag warning signs: new or worsening pain, swelling, bruising, fever, dark urine, marked weakness, or pain out of proportion to activity, which would warrant prompt re‑evaluation. Recommend a gradual progression of exercise intensity in future workouts to reduce the severity of DOMS. Review the medication list for any myotoxic agents (e.g., statins, antipsychotics) and advise cessation or consultation if present. Inquire about recent infections, menstrual cycle phase, and family history of muscular disorders, as these may influence symptom perception or risk of complications. Age: 24  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Sudden onset shortness of breath and right‑sided back pain during exertion  

Analysis: All three experts converged on the diagnosis of a right‑sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) based on the patient’s young age, smoking history, abrupt dyspnea, unilateral pleuritic pain, and decreased breath sounds on the right. The panel unanimously agreed that the condition is urgent and requires emergent evaluation, that red‑flag findings (tracheal deviation, hypotension, severe hypoxia, hemodynamic instability) would mandate immediate decompression, and that the primary differentials include pulmonary embolism, pleural effusion, pericarditis, asthma/bronchospasm, musculoskeletal strain, rib fracture, aortic dissection, and pneumonia. Consensus existed on upright chest X‑ray as the first‑line diagnostic test, with point‑of‑care thoracic ultrasound as an acceptable rapid alternative and chest CT reserved for equivocal cases or pre‑operative planning. Management consensus emphasized supplemental oxygen, cardiac and pulse‑ox monitoring, IV access, analgesia, and size‑based intervention (observation for small, needle aspiration for moderate‑to‑large or symptomatic, chest‑tube thoracostomy if aspiration fails or the patient destabilizes). All agreed that Emergency Medicine should lead initial care with early Pulmonology or Thoracic Surgery consultation for definitive management and recurrence risk assessment.  

Where consensus differed: Expert C initially classified the subclinical specialization as “Emergency,” whereas the aggregated majority label is Pulmonology; this was resolved in favor of Pulmonology. Expert A’s follow‑up answer was less detailed, while Experts B and C expanded on repeat imaging, smoking‑cessation counseling, activity restrictions, patient education, and evaluation for underlying lung disease. The outlier concerns raised during the rounds (assessment of height/body habitus, evaluation for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency or cystic lung disease, role of chest CT, repeat imaging before discharge, and explicit patient education) were incorporated into the final recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upright postero‑anterior chest X‑ray (with lateral view if needed); point‑of‑care thoracic ultrasound as an alternative; pulse‑oximetry and cardiac monitoring; intravenous access supplies; supplemental oxygen delivery devices; analgesics; equipment for needle aspiration (large‑bore catheter) and chest‑tube thoracostomy set; chest CT scanner (available if initial imaging is inconclusive or for surgical planning).  

Conclusion: Right‑sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations: Immediately place the patient on continuous cardiac and pulse‑oximetry monitoring and administer high‑flow supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ > 92 %. Obtain an upright chest X‑ray without delay; if the radiograph cannot be obtained promptly, perform a bedside thoracic ultrasound to confirm the presence of a pneumothorax. Assess the size of the pneumothorax on imaging; a rim of air < 2 cm and clinical stability support observation with oxygen, whereas a larger rim or persistent dyspnea warrants needle aspiration, and failure of aspiration, a large/expanding pneumothorax, or any sign of instability mandates chest‑tube thoracostomy. Continuously reassess for red‑flag signs (tracheal deviation, hypotension, JVP elevation, SpO₂ < 90 % despite oxygen, rapid respiratory distress) and be prepared to perform emergent needle decompression if they develop. Emergency Medicine should lead the acute management; request early consultation with Pulmonology (or Thoracic Surgery) for definitive decision‑making, especially if chest‑tube placement is needed or if surgical intervention may be considered.  

After initial stabilization, arrange a repeat chest X‑ray 24–48 hours later (or sooner if clinical change) to confirm lung re‑expansion before discharge. Provide comprehensive smoking‑cessation counseling, emphasizing that continued tobacco use markedly increases recurrence risk. Instruct the patient to avoid air travel, scuba diving, high‑altitude exposure, and heavy lifting until imaging confirms full resolution. Deliver clear discharge instructions describing warning symptoms of recurrence (sudden chest pain or dyspnea) and advise immediate return to the emergency department if they occur. Schedule outpatient follow‑up with Pulmonology within one week to review imaging, reinforce smoking cessation, discuss activity restrictions, and evaluate the need for preventive strategies such as pleurodesis if a second episode occurs.  

Because tall, thin habitus and underlying lung disorders (e.g., alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, apical blebs, cystic lung disease) are recognized risk factors for PSP, obtain a focused history of height, family history of early‑onset lung disease, and consider baseline laboratory testing (alpha‑1 antitrypsin level) and, if indicated, high‑resolution chest CT to identify blebs or bullae, particularly if the patient experiences recurrence or if surgical referral is contemplated.  

Notes: The patient’s mild hypoxemia (SpO₂ 94 % on room air) suggests at least a moderate pneumothorax; close monitoring is essential despite current hemodynamic stability. The runny nose is likely unrelated but should be documented.

Complaint: Collapse in the field after spraying organophosphate insecticide, with blurred vision, headache, profuse sweating, drooling, vomiting, and subsequent unresponsiveness
Analysis: The converged expert opinion identifies a severe acute organophosphate poisoning manifesting a classic cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia, hypotension, fasciculations, respiratory distress). All experts agree on the diagnosis, the need for emergent airway protection, and the core treatment sequence of decontamination, atropine titration, and pralidoxime infusion. Experts also concur on the essential supportive measures, required monitoring, and the spectrum of life‑threatening complications (respiratory failure, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, seizures, severe bradyarrhythmias, intermediate syndrome, delayed neuropathy). Divergence appears only in the classification labels: Expert A left the emergency type and subclinical fields blank, whereas Experts B and C assigned “Requires emergent care” and “Emergency”. Required diagnostic equipment/tests: arterial blood gas, serum electrolytes, serum glucose, complete blood count, serum cholinesterase level for trend, 12‑lead electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, bedside cardiac ultrasound if hemodynamic instability is suspected
Conclusion: Acute organophosphate poisoning causing a cholinergic crisis with imminent respiratory failure; requires immediate decontamination, airway protection, antidotal therapy, and intensive monitoring.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Remove all contaminated clothing and perform thorough skin decontamination while staff wear impermeable gloves, gowns, eye protection, and N95 or higher respirators; ensure environmental decontamination of the field and any equipment to prevent secondary exposure. Secure the airway with rapid sequence intubation and initiate mechanical ventilation. Begin atropine infusion and titrate upward until bronchial secretions are dry, recognizing that doses may need to exceed 10 mg per hour in severe cases; titration should be guided by secretion drying rather than heart rate or pupil size. Administer pralidoxime infusion as early as possible, ideally before the cholinesterase‑organophosphate complex ages, and continue for the recommended duration, adjusting if mixed carbamate exposure is suspected. Provide benzodiazepine (e.g., diazepam) if seizures occur or to mitigate central cholinergic activity. Give isotonic intravenous fluids and consider norepinephrine infusion for hypotension refractory to fluids and atropine. Continuously monitor cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, respiratory parameters, and serum potassium, as hypokalemia can exacerbate neuromuscular weakness. Obtain arterial blood gas and repeat electrolytes frequently to guide ventilation and metabolic support. Arrange toxicology, critical care, and pulmonology consultations for dosing guidance, ventilator management, and management of refractory bronchospasm or pulmonary edema. Admit to a monitored ICU bed for ongoing mechanical ventilation, atropine titration, pralidoxime infusion, and observation for intermediate syndrome (24‑96 h) and delayed organophosphate‑induced neuropathy (2‑3 weeks). Plan step‑down to a general ward only after neurologic and respiratory stability are confirmed.
Notes: The garlic‑like odor on the patient’s clothing is a rapid bedside clue to organophosphate exposure. Strict adherence to personal protective equipment and decontamination protocols is essential to protect healthcare workers from secondary contamination during resuscitation and ongoing care.

Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: Nocturia (waking to urinate 6 times per night) with weak urinary stream and need to strain to initiate voiding
Analysis: The panel unanimously identified benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) as the underlying cause of the patient’s lower urinary tract symptoms. Physical examination (enlarged, smooth prostate on DRE) and a PSA of 3.2 ng/mL support BPH and make prostate cancer less likely at this time, although the family history of prostate cancer warrants continued surveillance. All experts agreed that there are no red‑flag features (hematuria, infection, acute retention, severe pain, weight loss, or neurologic deficits), confirming a non‑emergent presentation. Consensus differed on the timing of urology referral: one expert advocated for immediate referral because of prostate size and family history, while the others recommended a trial of primary‑care medical therapy with referral only if symptoms persist, post‑void residual is high, or PSA/DRE becomes concerning. Additional points of divergence included the need to discuss anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation (raised by one expert) and the degree of emphasis on potential sleep‑apnea‑related nocturia. All agreed that avanafil may interact with α‑blockers and that blood pressure monitoring is required.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Bladder scanner or ultrasound for post‑void residual volume measurement, uroflowmetry to assess urinary flow rate, renal/bladder ultrasound if post‑void residual >200 mL or if hydronephrosis is suspected, repeat serum PSA in 12 months (or sooner if symptoms change), consider prostate MRI or biopsy only if PSA rises markedly or DRE becomes abnormal, basic metabolic panel to assess renal function if needed.
Conclusion: Benign prostatic hyperplasia causing bladder outlet obstruction; non‑emergent condition.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Initiate lifestyle measures (limit evening fluid intake, avoid caffeine and alcohol before bedtime). Start an α1‑adrenergic blocker (e.g., tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily) at a low dose and counsel the patient to monitor for dizziness, especially because he is taking avanafil; advise spacing the doses and standing up slowly. Discuss the modest benefit of PDE5 inhibition on LUTS but emphasize that avanafil is not a primary therapy for BPH. If symptoms do not improve after 4–6 weeks or if post‑void residual exceeds 200 mL, add a 5‑α‑reductase inhibitor (finasteride 5 mg daily) given the prostate size (~70 g) and PSA level. Arrange repeat PSA testing in one year and repeat DRE at that time. Re‑evaluate anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation in light of his CHA₂DS₂‑VASc score; aspirin alone may be insufficient for stroke prevention, and shared decision‑making regarding oral anticoagulants should occur. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea if nocturia persists despite urologic therapy, using a validated questionnaire or sleep study referral. Obtain post‑void residual measurement at the initial visit; if elevated, perform renal/bladder ultrasound to rule out hydronephrosis. Refer to urology promptly if any of the following occur: lack of symptom improvement after an adequate trial of medication, post‑void residual >200 mL, rising PSA (>4.0 ng/mL) or abnormal DRE, or development of any red‑flag symptom (hematuria, acute retention, weight loss, bone pain). 
Notes: Ensure patient education on medication side effects, importance of adherence, and when to seek urgent care (e.g., sudden inability to void, severe pain, fever). Document discussion of anticoagulation and obtain shared decision‑making documentation.

Complaint: Lethargy, confusion, and suspected opioid overdose with subsequent recurrent respiratory depression, bradycardia, and hypotension after initial naloxone response.  

Analysis: The Delphi panel converged on opioid toxicity as the primary diagnosis, emphasizing that the patient’s relapse into profound lethargy, bradycardia (HR 30 bpm), hypotension (BP 74/52 mm Hg), and hypoventilation after an initial naloxone reversal is most consistent with ongoing or delayed opioid absorption, likely from an extended‑release formulation. Expert C highlighted the possibility of co‑ingestion of other central nervous system depressants, particularly an unknown antidepressant that could be a tricyclic agent, as well as potential cardiotoxic antihypertensives (beta‑blocker, calcium‑channel blocker, clonidine). The panel noted that the absence of QRS widening or a described arrhythmia on the unavailable rhythm strip makes acute TCA toxicity less certain, but it cannot be excluded. Mild hypoglycemia (glucose 68 mg/dL) was deemed contributory but not the primary driver of the presentation. Experts A and B did not provide diagnostic classifications, indicating uncertainty but agreeing that the questionnaire supplied sufficient information for clinical decision‑making. The consensus therefore rests on Expert C’s detailed assessment, with acknowledgement of gaps due to unknown medication regimens and missing rhythm‑strip data.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac and pulse‑oximetry monitoring, bedside capnography, 12‑lead electrocardiogram, serum drug levels for tricyclic antidepressants, beta‑blockers, calcium‑channel blockers, ethanol and toxic alcohols, repeat arterial blood gas, serum electrolytes, liver function panel, and point‑of‑care glucose.  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing recurrent opioid‑induced respiratory and cardiovascular depression, likely compounded by an unknown co‑ingested medication that may be contributing to bradycardia and hypotension. Immediate continued opioid antagonism, hemodynamic support, and comprehensive toxicologic evaluation are required, followed by urgent psychiatric assessment for suicide risk.

Sex: Female  
Complaint: Right upper quadrant pain of 2 days duration, radiating to the right scapula, associated with nausea, vomiting, and low‑grade fever; positive Murphy sign on examination.  

Analysis: The clinical picture of post‑prandial RUQ pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and a positive Murphy sign together with ultrasound findings of gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (5 mm), pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy sign is diagnostic of acute calculous cholecystitis. All three experts concur on this diagnosis and on General Surgery as the definitive service. Consensus was reached that the case requires emergent care, meaning prompt admission, initiation of supportive therapy, and early surgical evaluation within the next 24–72 hours. A minority of experts initially described the situation as “urgent but not immediately life‑threatening” because the patient is hemodynamically stable and lacks peritoneal signs; however, the panel agreed that the presence of systemic inflammation (fever, imaging‑confirmed gallbladder inflammation) and obesity place the patient at risk for rapid progression, justifying emergent admission. The need for VTE prophylaxis and peri‑operative risk assessment was raised as an outlier by Expert B and subsequently incorporated into the consensus recommendations. Additional considerations highlighted during the rounds include obesity‑related gallstone risk and peri‑operative complications, the necessity of a pregnancy test in women of child‑bearing age, the importance of obtaining a baseline medication list and assessing comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, immunosuppression), and the value of serial abdominal examinations to detect evolving peritonitis. Red‑flag thresholds (fever > 101.5 °F, leukocytosis > 15 × 10⁹/L, worsening pain, new peritoneal signs, hypotension, tachycardia, mental status change, CBD > 6 mm, jaundice, Charcot triad, rising amylase/lipase) were agreed upon for escalation of care.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound (already performed); complete blood count with differential; comprehensive metabolic panel; liver function tests (AST, ALT, ALP, bilirubin); serum amylase and lipase; blood cultures if febrile; urine pregnancy test; review of current medications; consider MRCP or ERCP only if clinical or laboratory evidence suggests common bile duct obstruction or choledocholithiasis.  

Conclusion: Acute calculous cholecystitis in an obese 38‑year‑old woman, uncomplicated by jaundice or ductal dilation, requiring emergent admission and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  

Recommendations: Admit the patient promptly; keep NPO; initiate aggressive intravenous crystalloid hydration; provide analgesia with intravenous acetaminophen and short‑acting opioids as needed; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering gram‑negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g., ceftriaxone plus metronidazole or piperacillin‑tazobactam). Obtain the laboratory panel listed above and a urine pregnancy test before any radiologic study involving radiation or before surgery. Conduct a thorough medication reconciliation and assess comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, or immunosuppression to guide peri‑operative planning. Implement pharmacologic and mechanical venous thromboembolism prophylaxis given the patient’s obesity, and continue prophylaxis in the postoperative period as indicated. Schedule early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 24–72 hours of admission, ensuring the patient is optimized medically and surgically. Provide patient education on a low‑fat diet, gradual weight loss, avoidance of large fatty meals, and the importance of timely surgery. Instruct the patient to monitor for red‑flag symptoms (fever > 101.5 °F, increasing pain, jaundice, vomiting) and to seek immediate medical attention if they occur. Arrange for serial abdominal examinations during the hospital stay to detect any development of peritoneal signs. Plan postoperative follow‑up within two weeks to assess wound healing, reinforce lifestyle modifications, and evaluate for any delayed complications.  

Notes: The common bile duct measures 4 mm, which is within normal limits; therefore, routine pre‑operative ERCP is not indicated unless new evidence of obstruction emerges. Absence of documented leukocytosis does not exclude the diagnosis; a CBC should be obtained promptly to assess for infection.

Age: 35
Sex: Male
Complaint: Expanding erythematous annular rash on right thigh with mild systemic symptoms after removal of an engorged tick

Analysis: The presentation is classic for early localized Lyme disease (erythema migrans) in a highly endemic area (Connecticut) with a known Ixodes scapularis bite and systemic features (fatigue, headache, arthralgias, low‑grade fever). All experts agreed the condition is non‑emergent and can be managed in outpatient General Medicine. Consensus identified the need for prompt doxycycline therapy and education on red‑flag signs that would require urgent reassessment (neurologic, cardiac, severe arthritis, high‑grade fever, necrotic rash). Divergence arose regarding diagnostic testing: Expert B recommended baseline labs (CBC, renal/hepatic function) and optional ECG before doxycycline, whereas Expert C argued that no laboratory testing is required for classic erythema migrans because early serology is often negative. The final protocol incorporates both viewpoints by offering baseline labs and ECG as reasonable adjuncts without delaying treatment. Expert B also emphasized explicit assessment of doxycycline contraindications, which is reflected in the recommendations. Additional considerations from the round summary include the possibility of co‑infection (Anaplasma, Babesia) and the importance of tick‑prevention counseling.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Physical examination of skin lesion and joints; optional two‑tier serology (ELISA with Western blot) for documentation; baseline complete blood count; serum creatinine and liver function tests; baseline electrocardiogram if cardiac symptoms are present or as a precaution; tick identification (if available) to confirm Ixodes scapularis exposure.

Conclusion: Early localized Lyme disease (erythema migrans) requiring outpatient antibiotic therapy.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations: 
1. Initiate doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10–14 days as first‑line therapy; it also covers common co‑infections. 
2. If doxycycline is contraindicated (pregnancy, breastfeeding, age < 8 years, known allergy, severe renal/hepatic impairment), prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily for the same duration. 
3. Before starting doxycycline, assess for contraindications and obtain baseline CBC, serum creatinine, and liver enzymes; obtain an ECG if any cardiac symptoms are reported or as a precaution in this endemic setting. 
4. Do not delay antibiotic initiation for serology; obtain two‑tier serology only if documentation is desired or if the rash is atypical. 
5. Monitor for co‑infection: repeat CBC and consider PCR or serology for Anaplasma or Babesia if fever persists beyond 48 hours, if cytopenias develop, or if there is unexplained malaise. 
6. Educate the patient on red‑flag signs that mandate urgent reassessment: facial palsy, meningitic symptoms, new cardiac symptoms (palpitations, syncope, chest discomfort), large joint effusions, high‑grade fever, or rapidly expanding necrotic skin lesions. 
7. Schedule follow‑up in 2–4 weeks to evaluate rash resolution and symptom improvement; reinforce prevention measures and reassess for any new manifestations. 
8. Provide comprehensive tick‑bite prevention counseling: use EPA‑registered repellents (DEET, picaridin, or IR3535), wear permethrin‑treated clothing, perform thorough skin checks after outdoor activities, remove attached ticks promptly with fine‑tipped tweezers, and maintain yard landscaping to reduce tick habitat. 
9. Document that no Lyme vaccine is currently available in the United States and advise the patient to seek care promptly for any future rashes or systemic symptoms.

Notes: The high pre‑test probability due to endemic location and an engorged tick increases confidence in the clinical diagnosis. Co‑infection risk is notable in Connecticut; vigilance for persistent fever or laboratory abnormalities is warranted. Immunocompetent status reduces the likelihood of severe disease, but atypical erythema migrans presentations (multiple lesions, atypical morphology) should be recognized. Baseline labs and ECG are optional but recommended to ensure safe doxycycline use and to screen for silent cardiac involvement.

There is unanimous agreement that no red‑flag symptoms (fever, vomiting, bloody or mucous stools, poor feeding, weight loss, lethargy, abdominal distension, abnormal neurologic findings, dehydration) are present, making urgent evaluation unnecessary. Consensus also exists on the primary management setting (general pediatrics), the lack of need for immediate diagnostic testing, and the core non‑pharmacologic interventions (reassurance, soothing techniques, safe‑sleep counseling). Minor variations among experts involve optional adjuncts: Lactobacillus reuteri probiotic and maternal dairy‑elimination trial, both endorsed as low‑risk options.  

A point of divergence arose regarding the inclusion of metabolic disorders in the differential. Experts A and B considered them exceedingly unlikely and did not list them, whereas Expert C initially added them and, after reflecting on the outlier, retained them as a very rare consideration only if atypical or persistent features develop. This difference is noted to ensure that metabolic causes are kept in mind for atypical presentations but not pursued in the current classic colic scenario.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None at this time; investigations are reserved for the emergence of red‑flag signs or atypical clinical evolution.  

Conclusion: Infantile colic – a benign, self‑limited condition not requiring emergent care.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Provide parental reassurance and education about the self‑limited nature of colic; teach and demonstrate soothing strategies such as swaddling, rocking, white‑noise, pacifier use, and appropriate holding positions; reinforce safe‑sleep practices and counsel on the risk of shaken‑baby syndrome, offering coping resources for parental stress. Review and document feeding schedule, stool characteristics, urine output, sleep duration, growth trajectory, immunization status, and environmental factors that may influence crying. Offer a trial of Lactobacillus reuteri probiotic for breastfed infants and consider a maternal dairy‑elimination diet if cow’s milk protein allergy is suspected. Schedule a routine pediatric follow‑up within 1–2 weeks and give explicit safety‑net instructions to seek urgent care for any red‑flag symptoms (fever, vomiting especially bilious, blood or mucus in stool, poor feeding, lethargy, abdominal distension, decreased wet diapers, bulging fontanelle, seizures). If symptoms persist beyond the typical colic window, become more severe, or are accompanied by systemic signs, initiate further evaluation which may include metabolic screening, imaging, or specialist referral.  

Notes: Evening crying pattern and peak age of 6 weeks are typical for colic; normal growth and exam are reassuring. Family history of excessive infant crying may be relevant. Parental stress and support systems should be assessed and addressed. Metabolic disorders remain a very low‑probability differential and should be considered only in atypical or refractory cases.

Analysis: All three experts concur that the presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated acute cystitis, a lower urinary tract infection in a young, otherwise healthy woman. The absence of systemic signs, flank pain, or costovertebral angle tenderness excludes pyelonephritis and other emergent conditions, supporting the consensus that emergent care is not required. The agreed‑upon differentials include urethritis (including STI‑related), vaginitis, interstitial cystitis, chemical irritation, and pyelonephritis; however, vaginal symptoms make vaginitis less likely. Experts uniformly identified red‑flag features (fever, chills, flank pain, nausea/vomiting, hematuria, systemic infection) as absent. Diagnostic consensus is that a mid‑stream clean‑catch urine sample for dipstick/urinalysis is indicated; however, there was disagreement on routine urine culture—Expert A advocated routine culture to monitor resistance, whereas Experts B and C recommended culture only for atypical presentations or treatment failure. All experts agreed on primary‑care management and that specialist referral is reserved for recurrent infection, treatment failure, red flags, structural abnormalities, or confirmed pregnancy.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Mid‑stream clean‑catch urine collection kit, urine dipstick/urinalysis device, pregnancy test (urine or serum), optional urine culture (if symptoms are atypical, persist, or recur), STI screening tests as indicated by sexual history, and assessment for hematuria on dipstick.  

Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute cystitis (lower urinary tract infection).  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations: Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy with nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days or trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally twice daily for 3 days, selecting the agent based on local resistance patterns; if resistance is a concern or the patient is pregnant, consider a single dose of fosfomycin. Confirm pregnancy status before prescribing; avoid nitrofurantoin in the first trimester and near term, and avoid TMP‑SMX in the first trimester. Encourage increased oral fluid intake, advise short‑term use of an over‑the‑counter urinary analgesic such as phenazopyridine for symptom relief, and counsel the patient to void after intercourse, maintain adequate hydration, and avoid bladder irritants (caffeine, alcohol, spicy foods). Discuss contraception, noting that diaphragms and spermicides increase UTI risk and suggesting alternative methods if appropriate. Provide clear return precautions: seek care if fever, chills, flank or back pain, worsening dysuria, or no improvement within 48–72 hours. Arrange follow‑up in 3–5 days, either in person or via telehealth, to reassess symptoms; if symptoms persist, obtain a urine culture and adjust antibiotics according to sensitivities. Offer STI screening given recent sexual activity, even in the absence of vaginal discharge. If dipstick shows hematuria, schedule a repeat urinalysis after infection resolution to exclude other pathology. Maintain a low threshold to re‑evaluate for early pyelonephritis if new red‑flag symptoms develop. Refer to urology or obstetrics/gynecology for recurrent infections (>2–3 per year), treatment failure, identified structural abnormalities, or confirmed pregnancy requiring obstetric input.  

Notes: Emphasize antimicrobial stewardship by reserving routine culture for cases where initial therapy fails or atypical features are present. Document patient education and consent for prescribed medications.

Sex: Male  
Complaint: Yellowish, greasy‑appearing scales on the scalp present for ~2 weeks, thick in some areas; infant otherwise thriving.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as classic seborrheic dermatitis of infancy (cradle cap). Consensus was reached that the condition is benign, self‑limited, and does not constitute an emergency. Red‑flag features that would change urgency were agreed upon and include fever, poor feeding, weight loss, failure to thrive, extensive erythema, oozing, crusting, lymphadenopathy, neurologic signs (e.g., bulging fontanelle), or spread of the rash beyond the scalp. The primary differentials listed by the panel—atopic dermatitis, infantile psoriasis, tinea capitis, scabies, impetigo, neonatal lupus, metabolic or neurologic disorders—are to be considered only if atypical findings emerge. Divergence occurred regarding topical corticosteroid use: Expert A advised against any steroid in uncomplicated cases, whereas Experts B and C endorsed optional low‑potency steroids (e.g., 1 % hydrocortisone) if inflammation persists after conservative measures. Referral recommendations were aligned in that specialist input is reserved for atypical, refractory, or concerning presentations; Expert A emphasized that routine referral is unnecessary for classic cradle cap.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No laboratory, imaging, or skin‑biopsy studies are indicated for a classic presentation; diagnosis is clinical.  

Conclusion: Seborrheic dermatitis of infancy (cradle cap).  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Initiate gentle daily scalp cleansing with a mild baby shampoo, using a soft brush or fine‑toothed comb to loosen adherent scales; apply mineral oil or petroleum jelly before washing to soften thick crusts. Avoid harsh soaps, vigorous scrubbing, or excessive friction, which can irritate the skin. If mild inflammation or persistent thick scaling remains after 1–2 weeks of these measures, a short course of a low‑potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., 1 % hydrocortisone applied once daily for up to 5 days) may be used; routine steroid use is not required in the absence of inflammation, reflecting Expert A’s concern about unnecessary medication. Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial or fungal infection—such as increased erythema, oozing, crusting, or foul odor—and educate parents that cradle cap is not contagious and does not reflect poor hygiene. Provide reassurance that the condition is self‑limited, typically resolving by 6–12 months, and address parental anxiety by explaining the natural course and expected outcomes. Advise caregivers to seek medical review promptly if any red‑flag features develop or if the rash spreads to the face, ears, or diaper area, becomes pustular, or fails to improve after 3 weeks of appropriate home care. Referral to pediatric dermatology should be considered for atypical presentations, treatment failure, rapid progression, suspicion of alternative diagnoses (e.g., psoriasis, metabolic disorder, immunodeficiency), or confirmed secondary infection.  

Notes: Maternal seborrheic dermatitis can influence infant presentation; family history of atopic dermatitis or psoriasis may predispose to similar rashes but does not alter management of classic cradle cap. Topical antifungals are unnecessary unless a fungal infection is specifically identified.

Analysis: All three experts converged on the diagnosis of a minor (recurrent) aphthous ulcer, describing the lesion as a shallow, oval ulcer with a white‑yellow base and erythematous halo in a young adult without systemic symptoms. Consensus was reached that the condition is benign, self‑limited, and does not require emergent intervention. The experts uniformly identified red‑flag features that would necessitate further evaluation, including ulcer persistence beyond two weeks, increase in size or induration, multiplicity, fever, lymphadenopathy, weight loss, systemic manifestations (e.g., genital or ocular lesions), and a history of tobacco or heavy alcohol use.  

A point of divergence concerned the differential diagnosis. Expert A excluded early squamous cell carcinoma and oral candidiasis, deeming them unlikely without risk factors, whereas Experts B and C listed them as “less likely but possible” and recommended consideration only if the lesion persisted or atypical features emerged. The panel also differed slightly on the preferred initial specialty for referral: Expert B suggested ENT/oral‑medicine as the first referral option, while Experts A and C emphasized primary care (General Medicine) with specialist referral reserved for persistent or atypical cases. These differences were incorporated into the safety‑netting recommendations.  

Additional considerations raised during the Delphi rounds included recent dental procedures or ill‑fitting appliances, tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use, nutritional deficiencies (iron, folate, vitamin B12), immunocompromised states, medication‑induced ulceration, personal or family history of recurrent aphthous ulcers or Behçet’s disease, and the impact of stress, poor sleep, and suboptimal diet common in college students.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No immediate diagnostic equipment or laboratory tests are required. If red‑flag features develop or the ulcer persists >2 weeks, consider CBC, iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate levels, HSV PCR, and incisional biopsy for histopathology.  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with a minor recurrent aphthous ulcer (aphthous stomatitis), a benign and self‑limited condition.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations: Initiate self‑care and primary‑care management. Advise gentle oral hygiene, avoidance of mechanical trauma, and cessation of any irritant foods or dental appliances. Recommend saline or salt‑water rinses 3–4 times daily. Use a topical analgesic such as benzocaine or lidocaine gel for pain relief, and apply a short course of a topical corticosteroid (e.g., triamcinolone acetonide paste) to reduce inflammation. Counsel the patient on stress‑reduction techniques, adequate sleep, and a balanced diet rich in iron, folate, and vitamin B12; consider screening for nutritional deficiencies if ulcers become recurrent. Review medication history for agents known to cause oral ulceration and adjust if appropriate. Inquire about recent dental work, ill‑fitting prostheses, tobacco, alcohol, and recreational drug use; advise cessation or modification as needed.  

Schedule a follow‑up in 1–2 weeks to assess healing. Instruct the patient to seek prompt re‑evaluation if any red‑flag signs appear: ulcer persisting beyond two weeks, increase in size or induration, development of multiple lesions, fever, lymphadenopathy, unexplained weight loss, or new systemic symptoms (e.g., genital or ocular lesions). Should any of these occur, arrange referral to ENT/oral‑medicine for specialist assessment and consider the outlined laboratory investigations and possible biopsy.  

Notes: The patient’s stress and poor sleep are likely triggers; addressing these lifestyle factors is an integral part of management.
